Liquid glass architecture—encompassing **Water-Filled Glass (WFG)**, **Fluid Glass Façades (FGF)**, and **Optofluidic Building Envelopes**—transforms architectural glazing from static, passive insulation into dynamic, active thermodynamic and optical regulators.[1][2][3]

***

## Architectural Mechanics and Typology

Fluid-filled building envelopes circulate a fluid layer (typically conditioned water mixed with anti-freeze and biocides or tunable microfluidic dye matrices) within standard double or triple glazing cavities.[2][4]

```
  OUTSIDE ENVIRONMENT
   │   Incident Solar Irradiance (I_0)
   ▼
┌─────────────────────────┐  ◄── Exterior Glass Pane
│       Gas Cavity        │  ◄── Argon / Low-E Layer
├─────────────────────────┤  ◄── Middle Structural Pane
│   Fluid Flow Channel    │  ◄── Circulating Liquid Matrix (ṁ, T_f)
├─────────────────────────┤  ◄── Interior Glass Pane
│   Convective Interface  │
└─────────────────────────┘
   ▼
  INDOOR ENVIRONMENT (T_i)
```

The system splits into primary functional layers:
- **Outer Optical/Thermal Filter**: Absorbs broad-spectrum near-infrared (NIR) radiation directly at the boundary, capturing solar gains before entering the indoor volume.[1][2]
- **Inner Hydronic Loop**: Connected to building geothermal loops, floor heating, or low-grade thermal reservoirs, maintaining inner glass surface temperatures close to ambient comfort zones (\(20^\circ\text{C} - 24^\circ\text{C}\)).[3][5]

***

## Core Mathematical Formulations

### 1. Dynamic Heat Balance and Transmittance

For a water-flow glazing module of height \(H\) and width \(W\), the spatial 1D steady-state temperature profile of the fluid \(T_f(y)\) along the flow coordinate \(y \in [0, H]\) is governed by:

\[
\dot{m} C_p \frac{dT_f(y)}{dy} = W \left[ U_{out} \left(T_e - T_f(y)\right) + U_{in} \left(T_i - T_f(y)\right) + \alpha_{eq} I_0 \right]
\]

Where:
- \(\dot{m}\): Mass flow rate of the liquid (\(\text{kg}\cdot\text{s}^{-1}\)).[6]
- \(C_p\): Specific heat capacity of the circulating fluid (\(\approx 4184\text{ J}\cdot\text{kg}^{-1}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\) for water).
- \(T_e, T_i\): Outdoor and indoor ambient temperatures (\(\text{K}\)).
- \(U_{out}, U_{in}\): Thermal transmittances from the liquid layer to exterior and interior zones (\(\text{W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\)).[7][6]
- \(\alpha_{eq}\): Equivalent absorptance of the composite glass-liquid assembly.[7]
- \(I_0\): Incident solar irradiance (\(\text{W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\)).[6][7]

Integrating over the pane height \(H\) with inlet boundary condition \(T_f(0) = T_{in}\) yields the outlet fluid temperature:

\[
T_{out} = T_e^* + \left(T_{in} - T_e^*\right) \exp\left(-\frac{(U_{out} + U_{in}) W H}{\dot{m} C_p}\right)
\]

where the effective reference stagnation temperature \(T_e^*\) is:

\[
T_e^* = \frac{U_{out} T_e + U_{in} T_i + \alpha_{eq} I_0}{U_{out} + U_{in}}
\]

### 2. Net Indoor Heat Flux

The dynamic thermal flux \(q_{net}\) entering the building space is expressed as:

\[
q_{net} = U \left(T_e - T_i\right) + U_w \left(T_{in} - T_i\right) + g_{dyn} I_0
\]

- \(U\): Static equivalent thermal transmittance (\(\text{W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\cdot\text{K}^{-1}\)).[6]
- \(U_w\): Dynamic coupling coefficient between fluid flow and indoor space.[6]
- \(g_{dyn}\): Effective Solar Heat Gain Coefficient (SHGC), which drops from \(\approx 0.70\) (passive state) to under \(0.15\) under active fluid circulation and dye injection.[8][9]

***

## Thermal and Fluid Mechanics

### Dimensionless Hydrodynamic Parameters

The fluid layer operates in the laminar or low-Reynolds transitional regime to prevent optical distortion caused by turbulent vortices:[10]

\[
\text{Re} = \frac{\rho v D_h}{\mu} = \frac{2 \dot{m}}{\mu W}
\]

\[
\text{Gr} = \frac{g \beta \Delta T \delta^3}{\nu^2}, \quad \text{Ra} = \text{Gr} \cdot \text{Pr} = \frac{g \beta \Delta T \delta^3 \rho C_p}{\nu k_f}
\]

- \(\delta\): Liquid cavity thickness (\(\text{typically } 8 - 16\text{ mm}\)).
- \(\beta\): Thermal expansion coefficient of the fluid (\(\text{K}^{-1}\)).
- \(\text{Ra} < 10^3\): Pure conduction regime in the fluid, ensuring minimal convective turbulence and uniform clarity.[10]

***

## Performance Comparison Across Glazing Systems

| Glazing System Architecture | \(U\)-Value (\(\text{W}\cdot\text{m}^{-2}\text{K}^{-1}\)) | Dynamic SHGC (\(g\)) | Thermal Energy Recovery |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Standard Double Glazing (Air cavity) | \(2.70 - 2.90\) | \(0.70 - 0.76\) | None (Static) |
| Low-E Argon Triple Glazing | \(0.60 - 0.80\) | \(0.45 - 0.55\) | None (Static) |
| Active Water-Flow Glazing (WFG) | \(0.06 - 0.50\) [9][11] | \(0.12 - 0.65\) [7][9] | Direct Solar Thermal (\(\eta_0 \approx 0.65 - 0.74\)) [7] |
| Multilayer Optofluidic Facade | \(0.20 - 0.60\) | \(0.05 - 0.70\) [2] | Multi-band Spectral Absorption [2] |

***

## Structural and Material Engineering Constraints

- **Hydrostatic Load Management**: In multi-story façades, hydrostatic pressure builds up as \(P_h = \rho g H\). Panels require pressure-decoupled unitized sub-frames or internal balancing manifolds to prevent pane deflection and fringe birefringence.[11][12]
- **Anti-Biofouling and Anti-Freezing**: Closed loops incorporate glycol solutions (\(15\% - 30\%\) depending on exterior design temperature \(T_{e,min}\)) and sub-micron UV sterilization to avoid biological fouling and preserve optical transmittance (\(\tau_v > 85\%\)).
